name: Advaita Vedānta

tradition.text: Guru-paramparā from Nārāyaṇa through Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, Parāśara, Vyāsa and Śuka to Gauḍapāda, Govinda and Śaṅkara; Śaṅkara commonly dated 788–820 CE, and 509–477 BCE in the Kāñcī and Dvārakā maṭha reckonings

scholarly.text: Gauḍapāda c. 6th c. CE; Śaṅkara c. 700–750 CE (Hacker, Nakamura; others to c. 800); continuous commentarial tradition to the present

transmissions_received.what: the mahāvākyas and the Upaniṣadic teaching of the self
transmissions_received.evidence: all Advaita works are exegeses of the Upaniṣads

transmissions_received.what: hermeneutics (six marks of purport), theory of verbal knowledge, and the six means of knowledge in empirical matters
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāntasāra's six liṅgas; Vedāntaparibhāṣā's pramāṇa chapters

transmissions_received.what: the eight limbs as auxiliaries of nirvikalpa samādhi; vocabulary of samādhi
transmissions_received.evidence: Vedāntasāra; Aparokṣānubhūti's reinterpreted limbs; BSBh 2.1.3 accepts Yoga's practices while rejecting its dualism

transmissions_received.what: dialectical and (later) Navya-Nyāya technique
transmissions_received.evidence: Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya, Tattvapradīpikā, Advaitasiddhi

transmissions_received.what: vocabulary and dialectic of non-origination in Gauḍapāda's fourth prakaraṇa (scholarly hypothesis; the tradition denies dependence, cf. GK 4.99)
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis; see coverage C (owned by U49)

transmissions_given.what: the Daśanāmī sannyāsa order and the four āmnāya maṭhas founded, in the tradition's account, by Śaṅkara
Advaita doctrine and Daśanāmī (Purī) sannyāsa lineage (recent)
Advaita doctrine and Daśanāmī (Sarasvatī) sannyāsa (recent)
the Advaita prakaraṇa texts Ramaṇa rendered into Tamil (Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka, Ātmabodha) (recent)

distinctive_positions: Brahman alone is real (satya); the world is not ultimately real (mithyā); the individual self is not other than Brahman (Brahmajñānāvalīmālā 20; VC 20).
Bondage is superimposition (adhyāsa) of the not-self on the self and vice versa, which is called ignorance (avidyā) (BSBh introduction).
The world is an apparent transformation (vivarta) of Brahman, not a real transformation (pariṇāma).
Three levels of reality: ultimate (pāramārthika), empirical (vyāvahārika), illusory (prātibhāsika).
Liberation is not produced; it is the self's own nature revealed by knowledge alone; action cannot remove ignorance (Ātmabodha 3).
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is possible; the body continues until the karma that began it (prārabdha) is exhausted (BS 4.1.15, 4.1.19).
The qualified seeker (with the four qualifications) hears (śravaṇa), reflects (manana) and contemplates (nididhyāsana) the Upaniṣadic teaching.
Saguṇa Brahman (Īśvara) is real at the empirical level and the proper object of worship; nirguṇa Brahman is the ultimate.
Scripture teaches by provisional superimposition and subsequent retraction (adhyāropa-apavāda).
Post-Śaṅkara Advaita divides into the Vārttika (Sureśvara), Bhāmatī (Vācaspati) and Vivaraṇa (Prakāśātman) lines over the locus of ignorance and how the one appears as many.
summary: The Vedānta school of strict non-dualism: Brahman, pure consciousness without a second, is the self of all; the world of plurality is an appearance of Brahman through māyā/avidyā, real for empirical purposes but sublated by knowledge. Rooted in Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkya Kārikā and systematized by Śaṅkara's commentaries on the prasthāna-traya, it developed through Maṇḍana, Sureśvara, Padmapāda, Vācaspati and Prakāśātman into the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa lines, a dialectical literature (Śrīharṣa, Citsukha, Madhusūdana), popular manuals (Pañcadaśī, Vedāntasāra, Vedāntaparibhāṣā) and a living monastic order (Daśanāmī).

name: Aghora (Aghor panth; Aghorī and Aughaṛ ascetics)
regions: Varanasi (Kīnārām Sthal / Krīm Kuṇḍ at Śivālā; Parāo)

tradition.text: Kīnārām, born Vikrama 1658 (1601 CE) at Rāmgaṛh near Varanasi, lived to 1771 CE; Dattātreya is the ādiguru

scholarly.text: the Kīnārāmī lineage is attested from the 18th c.; any continuity with the medieval Kāpālikas is a scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Dattātreya as ādiguru; Girnar as the place of Kīnārām's vision
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition's account (Kīnārām hagiography).

transmissions_received.what: Kīnārām's first (Vaiṣṇava) initiation under Śivarām and the Rāma-devotional language of his works (Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl)
transmissions_received.evidence: the tradition's account; titles of Kīnārām's works.

transmissions_received.what: cremation-ground practice, skull bowl, transgression of purity rules
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis; not the tradition's own account.

transmissions_given.what: the Aghora lineage re-shaped toward social service (1961 onward)

distinctive_positions: Non-discrimination (abheda): nothing is to be shunned as impure; the aghora (the 'not-terrible') Śiva is present in what is feared and loathed.
Freedom from the eight fetters — disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste (the Kaula list, Kulārṇava 13.90) — is the mark of the free one.
The cremation ground (śmaśāna) is the place of practice; the skull bowl (khappar) is carried.
The guru is Śiva; the lineage descends from Dattātreya through Kālūrām and Kīnārām.
The ultimate is named also as Rām / nirguṇa (Kīnārām's works); the state sought is sahaja and unmanī.
Recent teachers (Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām) direct Aghora toward service of the sick and outcaste and rejection of caste distinctions.
summary: Aghora is the lineage of Śaiva ascetics centred on Bābā Kīnārām's seat at Krīm Kuṇḍ in Varanasi, who trace their teaching to Dattātreya through Bābā Kālūrām. Its ascetics practise in the cremation ground and cultivate non-discrimination (abheda), overcoming disgust, fear and the other fetters. Kīnārām's Hindi works (Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī) join this with devotion to Rām as the attributeless; in the twentieth century Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh and turned the lineage toward service. Practice details are secret and only summarised here.
notes: family 'vedic' follows the coverage-map grouping (A7, Śaiva lineages); it does not settle the tradition's own rejection of Vedic ritual authority (see dsp:natha-varna-and-ritual (Aghora shares the Nāth position)) nor its overlap with the Buddhist Mahāsiddhas (C; brw:natha-mahasiddha). Tradition's dates for Kīnārām are recorded as the tradition gives them; they are not independently confirmed.

name: Aitihāsikas (the legend-school of Vedic interpretation)
distinctive_positions: Vedic figures are persons of old narratives: Vṛtra is an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ (Nirukta 2.16); the Aśvins are two pious kings (Nirukta 12.1); Yama and Yamī are the twins born to Saraṇyū (Nirukta 12.10).
summary: Interpreters named in Yāska's Nirukta who read the hymns through old stories (itihāsa); known only from Yāska's reports.
notes: Known only through the Nirukta, which reports their views alongside the Nairuktas' own.

name: Ārādhya Śaiva (Andhra)

scholarly.text: from the 12th c. (Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya)

distinctive_positions: Wear the liṅga and worship Śiva exclusively while retaining the sacred thread and Vedic rites.
Look to Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya, contemporary of Basava, as their founding teacher.
summary: A Telugu-speaking Vīraśaiva group, traditionally brāhmaṇa, tracing itself to Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya; it combines liṅga-wearing and exclusive Śiva devotion with retention of Vedic rites and the sacred thread.
notes: Low confidence on current practice details; recorded as a side in dsp:virasaiva-veda-agama-authority.

name: Arthaśāstra (the science of statecraft and wealth)
distinctive_positions: Artha is foremost among the three aims, since dharma and kāma are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).

The four sciences are investigation (ānvīkṣikī — Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics (vārttā) and governance (daṇḍanīti); investigation is 'the lamp of all sciences' (Arthaśāstra 1.2.1–12).
summary: The śāstra of the second aim of life (artha): kingship, administration, law, diplomacy and wealth, represented by Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, which cites earlier schools (Mānavas, Bārhaspatyas, Auśanasas and others). Recorded here for its teaching on the aims of life and the order of the sciences.
notes: New lineage id (not in the registry) created by U02 for the puruṣārtha scope; the orchestrator may reassign.

name: Ārya Samāj

scholarly.text: founded 1875 CE

distinctive_positions: Only the four Saṃhitās are revealed (the Brāhmaṇas, Purāṇas and later texts are human works to be accepted only where they agree with them).
The Vedas teach one formless God; Agni, Indra and the other names denote that one God.
The Vedas contain no history of persons or places; their knowledge (and the sacred thread and Vedic study) is open to all, women and men of every birth.
Image worship and birth-based caste are rejected; the daily fire offering (havana/agnihotra) and Vedic study are kept.
summary: A Vedic-revival movement founded by Dayānanda Sarasvatī that reads the Saṃhitās as the sole revelation of one God; recorded here only for its reading of the Saṃhitās (recent, post-1800).
notes: Not in the registry; created by U01 because its founder's commentary is a major reading of the Saṃhitās. Positions recalled from memory (moderate). Flag for inclusion/exclusion (section H logic).

name: Atimārga

tradition.text: from Śiva's descent as Lakulin, the last of his 28 yoga-teacher incarnations (Liṅga P. 1.24; Kūrma P. 1.51)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (Lakulīśa) to c. 14th c. CE (last Kālāmukha and Pāśupata records); the name 'Atimārga' is used by Śaiva tantras from c. 6th–7th c.

transmissions_given.what: technical vocabulary (pati, paśu, pāśa), the five brahma-mantras, ash observances; the Mantramārga scriptures describe and rank the Atimārga below themselves
Kālāmukha temples and monasteries in Karnataka (disputed; see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva)

distinctive_positions: The Śaiva scriptures divide Śaiva revelation into the Atimārga and the Mantramārga; the Niśvāsamukha counts the Atimārga as the fourth of five 'streams' (laukika, vaidika, ādhyātmika, atimārga, mantra).
The Atimārga observances are for initiated ascetics and aim at liberation (duḥkhānta, the end of suffering); in the Pāśupata case initiation is restricted to brahmin men.
Its observances are defined as beyond the āśramas (atyāśrama: the Pāśupata) or beyond the world (lokātīta: the skull observance of the Lākulas and Kāpālikas).

The Svacchanda Tantra says the Atimārga lies 'beyond the states of the intellect' and that its skull-observers and Pāśupatas are not re-created, but it places their goals at levels below Śiva (Aiśvara pada, Dhruva).
The Lord (Paśupati, Rudra) is the independent cause; souls are eternal paśus; liberation is attained by the Lord's grace.
summary: The Atimārga ('path beyond') is the name the Śaiva scriptures give to the older of Śaivism's two great divisions, beside the Mantramārga ('path of mantras'). It comprises the Pāñcārthika Pāśupatas, who trace themselves to Lakulīśa and the Pāśupata Sūtra, the Lākulas (known in Karnataka as Kālāmukhas), and - in some sources and some modern accounts - the Kāpālikas or Somasiddhāntins. Its observances are ascetic and aim at liberation. Apart from the Pāśupata Sūtra with Kauṇḍinya's commentary and the Gaṇakārikā with its Ratnaṭīkā, it is known mainly from inscriptions, from the Mantramārga scriptures that describe it, and from opponents' reports.
notes: The division Atimārga/Mantramārga is the scriptures' own (Niśvāsa corpus; Svacchanda 11.182-190). Grouping the Kāpālikas as a third Atimārga division follows some scholarly reconstructions (Sanderson); other sources link the Kāpālika cult to the Mantramārga's Bhairava tantras. The Kūrma Purāṇa (2.37.146) lists 'Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula' together, with Vāma and Bhairava, as non-Vedic Śaiva teachings.

name: Bengali and Assamese Śākta tantra

tradition.text: Kāmarūpa is the seat where Satī's yoni fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42); Śiva himself revealed the tantras taught there

scholarly.text: Kālikā Purāṇa c. 10th–11th c.; Yoginī and Kāmākhyā Tantras c. 16th–17th c.; Kṛṣṇānanda c. late 16th–17th c.; the Śākta padāvalī 18th–19th c.

transmissions_received.what: Dakṣiṇakālī and the Mahāvidyās
transmissions_received.evidence: Tantrasāra quotes the Kālī Tantra and Muṇḍamālā

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual (pañcatattva, bhāvas)
transmissions_received.evidence: Kaulāvalīnirṇaya, Kulārṇava cited in the digests

transmissions_received.what: the Satī myth and the pīṭhas; Kāmākhyā
transmissions_received.evidence: Kālikā Purāṇa, Devī Bhāgavata

transmissions_given.what: Ramakrishna's Kālī devotion and his tantric sādhana under the Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī (recent)
shared songs and body-centred esoteric vocabulary (contested)

distinctive_positions: Kāmākhyā in Kāmarūpa is the seat where Satī's yoni fell; the Goddess there is the great vidyā in the form of the yoni and is all four aims of life (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4, 1.9).
The pīṭhas are the places where the parts of Satī's body fell and Śiva stays as a liṅga beside each (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.36-50).
Satī shows Śiva her ten Mahāvidyā forms, stationed in the ten directions, before going to Dakṣa's sacrifice (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa madhya 6.125-134).
Blood offering is taught (Kālikā Purāṇa ch. 67, 'rudhirādhyāya', summary only) together with substitutes (pumpkin, sugarcane, liquor as 'equal to' a victim) and prohibitions for brāhmaṇas.
The Dakṣiṇakālī form (four-armed, garland of heads, standing on Śiva) is set out in Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra, quoting the Kālī Tantra.
The Mahāvidyā mantras are 'siddha' vidyās needing no preliminary checks — which Kṛṣṇānanda reads as praise, not a rule (Tantrasāra, siddhādiśodhana).
Devotional Śāktism: the poet-saints sing to Kālī/Śyāmā as Mother, and to Umā in the homecoming (āgamanī) and farewell (vijayā) songs.
summary: The Śākta tantric culture of Kāmarūpa (Assam) and Bengal: the Kālikā Purāṇa on Kāmākhyā, the pīṭhas and the offerings; the Yoginī and Kāmākhyā Tantras; the Satī–Mahāvidyā myth of the Bṛhaddharma and Mahābhāgavata Purāṇas; the great digests of the 16th–19th centuries (Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra, Brahmānanda's Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī and Tārārahasya, Pūrṇānanda's Śrītattvacintāmaṇi and Śyāmārahasya, Sarvānanda's Sarvollāsa, the Prāṇatoṣiṇī); the Tārā cult of Tārāpīṭh; and the Śākta devotional songs of Rāmprasād Sen and Kamalākānta.

name: Early Bhāgavata devotion (the Nārāyaṇīya / Sātvata–Ekāntika dharma)
regions: Mathurā and the Śūrasena country; Vidiśā (Besnagar); Rajasthan (Ghosuṇḍī); western Deccan (Nānāghāṭ) — on the scholarly (inscriptional) evidence
Badarī (Nara–Nārāyaṇa's hermitage) and Śvetadvīpa in the tradition's account

tradition.text: the Sātvata dharma was given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and handed down (MBh 12.336)

scholarly.text: worship of Vāsudeva attested from c. 4th–2nd c. BCE (Pāṇini 4.3.98 'vāsudevaka'; Heliodorus's Garuḍa pillar at Besnagar, late 2nd c. BCE, whose donor calls himself a bhāgavata; the Ghosuṇḍī and Nānāghāṭ inscriptions naming Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, c. 1st c. BCE); the Nārāyaṇīya's theology c. 1st c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories in which the fourfold form is stated
transmissions_received.evidence: 12.326.100 calls the teaching 'made by Sāṃkhya-yoga, called Pañcarātra'

transmissions_received.what: sacrificial worship reoriented to Nārāyaṇa; the Vedas as part of the teaching
transmissions_received.evidence: Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323–324); 12.336.76 joins Sāṃkhya-yoga, the Vedāraṇyaka and Pañcarātra

transmissions_given.what: the fourfold form (caturvyūha) and the Sātvata worship of Vāsudeva
lists of the Lord's manifestations (prādurbhāva/avatāra) and Kṛṣṇa devotion (Harivaṃśa, Bhāgavata and Viṣṇu Purāṇas)
devotion to Nārāyaṇa/Kṛṣṇa as the one refuge
the Gītā, Nārāyaṇīya and Viṣṇu Sahasranāma as authorities for Nārāyaṇa's supremacy and surrender

distinctive_positions: Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva is the one supreme Lord, the knower of the field whose self is without guṇas (12.326.38).
The fourfold form (caturvyūha): from Vāsudeva comes Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), from him Pradyumna (the mind), from him Aniruddha (the ego), from whom Brahmā arises (12.326.68–69; 12.327.26).
The liberated ascend through the sun into Aniruddha, Pradyumna and Saṃkarṣaṇa and finally Vāsudeva; the one-pointed devotees (ekāntins) enter Vāsudeva directly (12.332.13–18; 12.336.3).
The Lord appears again and again (prādurbhāva) as Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi and at Mathurā, and earlier as Haṃsa and Hayaśiras (12.326.71–94); cf. BhG 4.7–8.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti), worship according to rule without desire, is the highest dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga (12.336.4, 12.336.69).
Worship by sacrifice without slaughter (Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice; the dispute over 'aja' as goat or grain, 12.323–324).
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas and Pāśupata are distinct systems, yet Nārāyaṇa is the culmination seen in all (12.337.59–67).
Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).
The teaching Kṛṣṇa gave Arjuna before the battle is this dharma (12.336.8); taking refuge in the Lord alone frees from all sins (BhG 18.66), even for women, vaiśyas and śūdras (BhG 9.32).
summary: The early devotional religion of Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) as found in the Nārāyaṇīya of the Mahābhārata, the Bhagavad Gītā's teaching of devotion and surrender, the Harivaṃśa and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma: exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to one Lord in a fourfold form, worship without animal sacrifice, and the Lord's repeated appearances to protect dharma. It flows into the Pāñcarātra, the Purāṇic Vaiṣṇavism and the later Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas.
notes: Owned by U05. Scholarly (labeled) observation: the three 'immortal steps' of Heliodorus's inscription — self-restraint, renunciation, heedfulness (dama, cāga, apramāda) — match the triad 'damas tyāgo 'pramādaś ca' at MBh 11.7.19 and 5.43.14.

name: Bhāmatī school (Bhāmatī-prasthāna)

scholarly.text: From Vācaspati Miśra (9th or 10th c.) through Amalānanda (13th c.) and Appayya Dīkṣita (16th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Maṇḍana Miśra's Brahmasiddhi, which Vācaspati followed on several points
transmissions_received.evidence: Vācaspati also commented on the Brahmasiddhi (Tattvasamīkṣā, lost)

distinctive_positions: Ignorance resides in the individual selves (jīvāśrita) and has Brahman as its object; the mutual dependence of jīva and avidyā is beginningless like seed and sprout.
Avidyās are many, one for each jīva; hence many jīvas (aneka-jīva).
Limitation theory (avaccheda-vāda): the jīva is Brahman as delimited by the inner organ, as space is delimited by a pot.
The Upaniṣadic sentence yields mediate (parokṣa) knowledge; the mind purified by sustained contemplation is the instrument of direct realization.
Contemplation (nididhyāsana, prasaṅkhyāna) is the principal means; hearing and reflection are auxiliaries.
Vedic works produce the desire to know (vividiṣā), not knowledge itself.
summary: The line of post-Śaṅkara Advaita founded on Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī, drawing on Maṇḍana Miśra, continued by Amalānanda's Kalpataru and Appayya Dīkṣita's Parimala. It places ignorance in the individual selves, explains the jīva by limitation, admits many jīvas, and holds that the mind, perfected by contemplation, turns the verbal knowledge of the mahāvākya into direct realization.

name: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā
regions: North and South India; strong later centres at Vārāṇasī (Khaṇḍadeva's circle), Mithilā, the Tamil country and Kerala (Mānameyodaya)

scholarly.text: from Kumārila (c. 6th–7th c. CE) to the present; the dominant school of Mīmāṃsā

transmissions_given.what: six means of knowledge (including postulation and non-apprehension), used by Advaita for empirical matters (e.g. Vedāntaparibhāṣā)

distinctive_positions: Six means of knowledge: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation (arthāpatti) and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi / abhāva-pramāṇa).
Sentence meaning by 'connection of the expressed' (abhihitānvaya): words first convey their own meanings, which then combine into the sentence meaning (Śabara on MS 1.1.25; ŚV vākya 342–343).
Error as apprehension of a thing as other than it is (viparītakhyāti): the related items are real, only their relation is unreal (Śāstradīpikā).
Cognition is not itself perceived; it is inferred from the 'knownness' (jñātatā / prākaṭya) it produces in the object.
The injunctive suffix expresses a verbal efficient force (śābdī bhāvanā) that prompts the person's own effort (ārthī bhāvanā) with its three expectancies: what, by what, how.
Obligatory and occasional rites destroy past sin and avert the demerit of omission (Tantravārttika).

Liberation: the one seeking release avoids desire-prompted and prohibited acts, performs obligatory and occasional rites, knows the self, and when past karma is exhausted by experience no new body arises (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 102–111).
Pārthasārathi: liberation is the absolute dissolution of the threefold bond (body, senses, objects) and is without bliss; some Bhāṭṭas held that the liberated self enjoys its innate bliss.
Words are the eternal letters; the grammarians' sphoṭa is superfluous (ŚV sphoṭavāda).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati and a total dissolution of the world (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116).
summary: The school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, built on his Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā and developed by Maṇḍana Miśra, Umbeka, Sucarita, Pārthasārathi Miśra and, later, Khaṇḍadeva, Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara. It defends six means of knowledge, the abhihitānvaya theory of sentence meaning, the bhāvanā theory of injunction, and a realist ontology; its epistemology was adopted by Advaita Vedānta for worldly matters.
notes: 'Tautātita-mata' (the doctrine of Tutāta, an epithet of Kumārila) is attested in the title of Bhavadeva's Tautātitamatatilaka; low confidence on the epithet's general currency. Maṇḍana Miśra is placed here by tradition (as Kumārila's pupil) though several of his positions differ (e.g. iṣṭasādhanatā as the meaning of injunction; defence of sphoṭa).

name: Bhedābheda Vedānta (Bhāskara's school and the early difference-and-non-difference Vedāntins)

scholarly.text: pre-Śaṅkara (Bhartṛprapañca) to 16th c. (Vijñānabhikṣu); Bhāskara c. 8th–9th c. CE

transmissions_given.what: the pariṇāma (real transformation) reading of the Brahma Sūtras and the jīva-as-part (aṃśa) doctrine, which Rāmānuja received through his first teacher Yādavaprakāśa and then criticised
the general bhedābheda frame (difference and non-difference of Brahman, souls and world)

distinctive_positions: Brahman is both different and non-different from the individual souls and the world: one as cause, many as effect.
The world is a real transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman or of its power (śakti), not an appearance (vivarta).
Bhāskara: the difference of the soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural (aupādhika-bhedābheda).
Yādavaprakāśa: both difference and non-difference are natural (svābhāvika-bhedābheda); Brahman itself becomes Īśvara, souls and matter.
Liberation requires knowledge combined with lifelong ritual and social duty (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) — Bhartṛprapañca, Bhāskara.
Bhāskara denies liberation while living (jīvanmukti): release comes when the body, a real adjunct, falls away.
Bhāskara attacks Śaṅkara's doctrine of māyā as a teaching of the Mahāyāna Buddhists.
Vijñānabhikṣu (16th c.) restates the position as avibhāga (non-separation) of souls and prakṛti from Brahman, harmonising Vedānta with Sāṃkhya-Yoga.
summary: The oldest continuous current of Brahma Sūtra interpretation: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world, which are its real transformations. Known for Bhartṛprapañca only through fragments reported by his Advaita critics; its classic statement is Bhāskara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya; Yādavaprakāśa (Rāmānuja's first teacher) gave a 'natural' version; Vijñānabhikṣu revived the frame in the 16th c. No living order continues the school; its ideas passed into the Vaiṣṇava Vedāntas.

name: Bhūta stream (tantras for spirits)
distinctive_positions: Tantras for the control and exorcism of spirits (bhūta, graha), issued from the western face (Sadyojāta) (Kāmika pūrva 1.26; the Śrīkaṇṭhīya as quoted by Jayaratha: 'in the west, the Bhūta tantras').
summary: The Śaiva scriptural stream concerned with spirit-possession and exorcism; known mostly from lists and fragments.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08; the Kāmika's printed text names twenty Bhūta tantras 'beginning with Kaula' (reading uncertain). family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Dāyabhāga school of Dharmaśāstra (Bengal)
distinctive_positions: Ownership of the father's property passes to the heirs only on the father's death or fall (uparamasvatva), not by birth.
Heirship follows capacity to benefit the deceased by ancestral offerings (piṇḍa).
summary: The Bengal tradition following Jīmūtavāhana's Dāyabhāga (c. 12th c.), which argues against the Mitākṣarā on inheritance and the basis of kinship.

name: Dharmaśāstra (the science of dharma; Dharmasūtra and Smṛti)
regions: Āryāvarta and Madhyadeśa (the land defined in MDh 2.17–24 and VDh 1.8–9)

tradition.text: Manu Svāyambhuva received dharma from Svayambhū at the beginning of creation and taught it to the seers through Bhṛgu (MDh 1.58–60); each world-age has its own authoritative code (Parāśarasmṛti 1.24: Manu in Kṛta, Gautama in Tretā, Śaṅkha-Likhita in Dvāpara, Parāśara in Kali).

scholarly.text: Dharmasūtras c. 3rd–1st c. BCE; metrical smṛtis c. 2nd c. BCE – 1st millennium CE; commentaries and digests c. 8th–18th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the Dharmasūtras as the dharma-portion of the Kalpasūtras
transmissions_received.evidence: Āpastamba and Baudhāyana Kalpasūtras contain their Dharmasūtras

transmissions_received.what: the Brāhmaṇa doctrines of the debts (TS 6.3.10.5; ŚB 1.7.2.1), the five great sacrifices (ŚB 11.5.6.1) and upanayana (ŚB 11.5.4)
transmissions_received.evidence: direct parallels

transmissions_received.what: rules of interpretation (nyāya) applied to conflicting smṛti texts in the commentaries and digests
transmissions_received.evidence: explicit use of Mīmāṃsā maxims by Medhātithi, Vijñāneśvara, Jīmūtavāhana

transmissions_received.what: the teaching of the self and its knowledge placed at the summit of dharma (MDh 12.85; YS 1.8; ĀpDh 1.8.22–23)
transmissions_received.evidence: doctrinal parallels

transmissions_given.what: saṃskāra, śrāddha and prāyaścitta rules re-used and expanded in the Purāṇas
rules for the renouncer (MDh 6; VDh 10; YS 3) taken up by the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads and the ascetic orders

distinctive_positions: The sources of dharma are the whole Veda, the recollection (smṛti) and conduct of those who know it, the practice of good people (sadācāra) and what satisfies oneself (MDh 2.6, 2.12; YS 1.7 adds desire born of right intention); where the Veda is silent, the agreement of those who know dharma is authoritative (ĀpDh 1.1.1.2).

Dharma is specified by class (varṇa) and life-stage (āśrama); alongside these stands a dharma common to all four classes — non-injury, truth, not stealing, purity and restraint of the senses (MDh 10.63; YS 1.122).
A person is born owing three debts — to the seers, the gods and the ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5; four in ŚB 1.7.2.1) — and must discharge them before setting the mind on liberation (MDh 6.35–37).

The householder supports the other orders as air supports living beings (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90); whether the celibate orders are a free choice, a sequence, or not Vedic at all is disputed within the tradition (GDh 3.1, 3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27; VDh 7.3; MDh 6).
Life is consecrated by rites (saṃskāra) from conception to cremation, and sins are removed by expiation, confession, remorse, austerity and recitation (MDh 2.26–28; 11.227–229).
The highest dharma is seeing the self by yoga (YS 1.8); knowledge of the self is the highest of all practices, by which immortality is won (MDh 12.85).
Acts of mind, speech and body bear fruit in rebirth, and the three guṇas govern the resulting destinies (MDh 12.3–51).
Dharma differs from age to age (MDh 1.81–86; Parāśarasmṛti 1.24); later authorities list practices forbidden in the Kali age (kalivarjya).

The customs of regions, castes and families are authoritative where they do not conflict with the Veda (GDh 11.20; ĀśGS 1.7.1); whether regional customs that the śiṣṭas disapprove of are valid is debated (BDh 1.1.2.1–8).
summary: The literature and learned tradition that set out dharma — ritual, moral, social and legal duty — for the twice-born and for all: the Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha; the metrical smṛtis of Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Viṣṇu, Parāśara, Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana; and the commentaries and digests (nibandha) built on them. Its core teachings are the four classes and four life-stages, the four aims of life, the three debts, the five great daily sacrifices, the rites of passage from conception to cremation, the ancestral offerings, purity and impurity, expiation, kingship and law, and — at its summit — self-knowledge and liberation.

name: Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda; the Mādhva sampradāya)
alt_names: Brahma-sampradāya (its place in the later scheme of four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas)

tradition.text: the tradition traces the teaching to Nārāyaṇa (as Haṃsa) through Brahmā and a line of teachers; Vyāsa (an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa) fixed it in the Brahmasūtras; in the Kali age Madhva, the third avatāra of Vāyu, re-proclaimed it

scholarly.text: founded by Madhva in the 13th c. CE; living

transmissions_received.what: the Brahmasūtras as the root text, commented on by Madhva
transmissions_received.evidence: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, Anuvyākhyāna, Nyāyavivaraṇa, Aṇubhāṣya

transmissions_received.what: ten principal Upaniṣads, read as teaching difference and Viṣṇu's supremacy
transmissions_received.evidence: Madhva's ten Upaniṣad bhāṣyas

transmissions_received.what: the Pañcarātra accepted as valid scripture (sadāgama); mantra and worship lore
transmissions_received.evidence: Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1 (list of sadāgamas); Tantrasārasaṅgraha

transmissions_received.what: the Mahābhārata and the Gītā as scripture of the highest rank
transmissions_received.evidence: Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya; Gītābhāṣya; Gītātātparya-nirṇaya

transmissions_received.what: Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas insofar as they agree with the sadāgamas
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhāgavata-tātparya-nirṇaya; Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1

transmissions_received.what: authorless Veda, intrinsic validity, the marks of purport (upakrama etc.) — adapted
transmissions_received.evidence: Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1; Rāghavendra's Bhāṭṭasaṅgraha

transmissions_received.what: debate theory and logical vocabulary — adopted in part and criticized
transmissions_received.evidence: Kathālakṣaṇa; Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Vyāsatīrtha's Tarkatāṇḍava

transmissions_given.what: Dvaita doctrine (Hari's supremacy, gradation of souls) sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas, several of them disciples of Mādhva ascetics (Śrīpādarāja, Vyāsatīrtha, Vādirāja)
the Gauḍīya tradition claims descent from Madhva's line through Mādhavendra Purī; the claim is disputed (see brw:dvaita-gaudiya-parampara)

distinctive_positions: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa, Hari) alone is independent (svatantra); Lakṣmī, all souls, matter, time and the Veda are dependent (paratantra) on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1; Tattvaviveka 1).
Five real and eternal differences (pañca-bheda) — God–soul, God–matter, soul–soul, soul–matter, matter–matter — hold in every state, including liberation (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 1.68–71).
The world is real (satya); the Advaita doctrines of māyā, the world's falsity (mithyātva) and the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) are refuted (the ten prakaraṇas; Nyāyāmṛta).

Souls are innately graded (tāratamya) and fall into three classes — fit for liberation (mukti-yogya), ever-transmigrating (nitya-saṃsārin), fit for blinding darkness (tamo-yogya); a soul's fitness is beginningless and unalterable (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 4–7; MBTN 1.86–95).
Liberation is the soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss, graded even among the liberated (ānanda-tāratamya), in eternal difference from and dependence on Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu is full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of every defect; 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities; his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are not different from him (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 3).
Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge there is no abundant grace (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.1).
Bhakti is firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness (MBTN 1.85); it continues in liberation as eternal bliss (MBTN 1.104).

Three means of valid knowledge — perception, inference, authoritative word; perception is sevenfold, the witness (sākṣin) plus six senses; what the sākṣin establishes is never sublated (Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Anuvyākhyāna).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa) is the highest of souls; grace descends through the higher beings; Madhva is Vāyu's third avatāra after Hanumān and Bhīma (MBTN 32.162–166).
God is the efficient cause of the world, not its material cause; prakṛti is the material cause.

All words, letters and scriptures in their primary sense designate Viṣṇu; the Veda is authorless; valid scripture (sadāgama) is the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas that agree with them (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God — dependent on and similar to its original (bimba), and eternally distinct from it.
Chāndogya 6.8.7 is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), taught nine times with examples to show difference (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
summary: The Vedānta school founded by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called by its adherents Tattvavāda, 'the doctrine of reality'. It teaches that Viṣṇu alone is the independent reality, that souls and matter are real, dependent and eternally distinct from him and from one another (the five differences), that souls are innately graded, and that liberation — the soul's enjoyment of its own bliss in Viṣṇu's presence — comes only by his grace, won through knowledge and devotion. Its classical literature runs from Madhva's thirty-seven works through Jayatīrtha's commentaries and Vyāsatīrtha's polemics to Rāghavendra; it is carried by ascetic maṭhas (the eight of Uḍupi with their biennial rotation of Kṛṣṇa worship, and the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) and was sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas.
notes: The tradition's teacher line before Madhva (the 'Haṃsa paramparā': Haṃsa-Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the Sanaka group, Durvāsas, then a line of ascetics ending in Acyutaprekṣa) is recalled here only in outline; the intermediate names are not listed because they were not verified in this pass. A traditional verse likens the doctrine to a tree: seed sown by Vyāsa in the soil of śruti, sprouted by Madhva, branched by Jayatīrtha, leaved by Vyāsarāja, flowered by Vijayīndra and fruited by Rāghavendra (quoted as a preface verse in a modern edition in the raw_etexts corpus; author not identified). Further maṭhas (Śrīpādarāja maṭha at Mulbagal, Subrahmaṇya, Bhīmanakaṭṭe, Bhaṇḍārakeri; the Gauḍa Sārasvata Mādhva maṭhas of Kāśī and Gokarṇa-Partagāḷī) are mentioned without separate entries — details not verified.

name: Dvaitādvaita (Nimbārka Sampradāya)

tradition.text: founded by Haṃsa (Viṣṇu) and transmitted through the four Kumāras and Nārada to Nimbārka in a former age

scholarly.text: Nimbārka variously dated 7th–13th c.; many place him c. 12th–13th c.

transmissions_given.what: Keśava Kāśmīrin's Kramadīpikā (Kṛṣṇa-mantra liturgy) used in Gauḍīya ritual codes (low confidence)
the Haridāsī tradition of Svāmī Haridās is sometimes affiliated to the Nimbārka line (contested)

distinctive_positions: Natural (svābhāvika) difference-and-non-difference: souls and world are both different and non-different from Brahman by their very nature, like sun and rays or snake and coils (BS 3.2.27).
Three realities: cit (souls), acit (non-conscious: prākṛta, aprākṛta, kāla) and Īśvara.
Brahman is Kṛṣṇa, free of all faults and a mass of auspicious qualities, worshipped together with Rādhā on his left (Daśaślokī 4–5): yugala-upāsanā.
The soul is atomic, a knower, a part (aṃśa) of the Lord and wholly dependent on him; infinite in number.
Five things to be known (arthapañcaka): the worshipped, the worshipper, the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, the obstacles.
Five means (upāya): karma, vidyā, upāsanā (dhyāna), prapatti (surrender) and gurūpasatti (surrender to the teacher).
Liberation is attainment of the Lord's nature and service after death, with difference preserved; grace arises for the humble (Daśaślokī 9).
summary: The Vaiṣṇava Vedānta of Nimbārka: Brahman as Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā, and souls and matter as his naturally different-yet-non-different powers. Its root texts are Nimbārka's brief Brahma Sūtra commentary (Vedāntapārijātasaurabha) and the ten-verse Daśaślokī, expanded by Śrīnivāsa's Vedāntakaustubha and Keśava Kāśmīrin's Kaustubhaprabhā; Śrī Bhaṭṭa and Harivyāsadeva gave it Braj-language devotional poetry. It counts itself one of the four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas (the Sanakādi/Kumāra line) and lives today with seats at Salemabad and in Braj.

name: Epic teaching (the Mahābhārata's Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Mokṣadharma milieu)
regions: northern India — the epics' settings: Kurukṣetra, Hāstinapura, Indraprastha, Mithilā (Videha), Naimiṣa forest, Badarī, Ayodhyā

tradition.text: the Kurukṣetra war and Vyāsa's composition at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali yugas (Kali traditionally from 3102 BCE); the Rāmāyaṇa in the earlier Tretā yuga

scholarly.text: the epic teaching layers c. 4th c. BCE – 4th c. CE

transmissions_received.what: the imperishable self and Brahman, the hierarchy of senses, mind and intellect, the paths after death, and whole verses
the sacrificial frame (yajña) and the wheel of sacrifice, reinterpreted inwardly
transmissions_received.evidence: BhG 3.9–16; 4.24–33; Anugītā 14.20–24 (the inner sacrifice of the senses)

transmissions_received.what: the enumeration of principles and the discrimination of puruṣa from prakṛti, in Kapila's line
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account: Pañcaśikha, 'Āsuri's first disciple', teaches Janadeva Janaka (MBh 12.211.6–18); Kapila named as proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60)

transmissions_given.what: the Bhagavad Gītā as the smṛti-prasthāna commented on by every Vedānta school
pre-classical Sāṃkhya enumerations (24/25/26 principles) — on the scholarly account, precursors of Īśvarakṛṣṇa's system
epic yoga vocabulary: dhāraṇā, the five faults of yoga, yoga-power (yogabala), the first dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra
cosmology of the ages and dissolution, lists of the Lord's manifestations, dharma teaching
the Gītā through Jñāneśvar's Jñāneśvarī
Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and the Anuśāsana's teaching on gifts, fasts and funerary offerings

distinctive_positions: Action is unavoidable for the embodied; what binds is attachment to the fruit, not action itself (BhG 3.5, 2.47, 18.11).
Several disciplines — knowledge (sāṃkhya), disciplined action (yoga), meditation and devotion — lead to one goal; 'one who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, sees' (BhG 3.3, 5.4–5, 13.24–25).
The self in the body is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.12–30).
Prakṛti with its three guṇas is the agent of all action; the puruṣa experiences and witnesses (BhG 3.27, 13.19–22).
The principles are counted as 24 with the puruṣa as 25th, and the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla and Yājñavalkya dialogues add a 26th, the awakened (MBh 12.294–296, 12.306).
Sāṃkhya and Yoga differ in method — Yoga relies on direct perception and argues that without a Lord no one is freed; Sāṃkhya relies on the teaching of the śāstra — yet both are true (MBh 12.289.3–7).
Dharma is subtle: conduct, not birth alone, is said to make a brāhmaṇa (3.177.16, 12.181.10), while the duties of the varṇas are also upheld (BhG 18.41–48; 12.60).
Non-cruelty (ānṛśaṃsya) and non-violence (ahiṃsā) are called the highest dharma (3.297.55; 1.11.12; 13.116), alongside the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war (BhG 2.31–33).
Liberation (brahmanirvāṇa, entering the Lord) can be won in this life by one whose mind rests in equality (BhG 5.19, 5.26, 2.72).

Time (kāla), nature (svabhāva), fate (daiva) and human effort are debated as causes; the Gītā counts daiva as one of five causes of action (18.14) and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not succeed without effort (13.6.7).
Dharma, artha and kāma are one whole (trivarga) grounded in dharma; 'from dharma come artha and kāma — why is it not practised?' (18.5.49).
summary: The teaching layer of the two Sanskrit epics, above all the Mahābhārata: the Bhagavad Gītā, Bhīṣma's instruction in the Śāntiparvan (Rājadharma, Āpaddharma, Mokṣadharma) and Anuśāsanaparvan, the Anugītā, the Sanatsujātīya, Vidura's counsel, the Yakṣa's questions, Mārkaṇḍeya's discourses, and the dharma teaching of the Rāmāyaṇa. It is not a school with a single doctrine but a milieu in which Upaniṣadic, early Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Vedic ritual, devotional (Bhāgavata) and ascetic ideas are set side by side in dialogues, and which later schools (Vedānta, classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the Purāṇas, bhakti traditions) all claim as authority.
notes: Owned by U05. 'Lineage' here names a teaching milieu (a body of texts and dialogues), not an initiatory succession; the tradition itself names chains of transmission within it (BhG 4.1–3; 12.211; 12.336 for the Sātvata dharma).

name: Gāruḍa stream (tantras of Garuḍa)
distinctive_positions: Mantras of Garuḍa and associated goddesses (e.g. Tvaritā) used against snake-poison and other poisons.
Issued from the eastern (Tatpuruṣa) face of Sadāśiva (Kāmika pūrva 1.21, 1.24; Śrīkaṇṭhīya as quoted by Jayaratha).
summary: The Śaiva scriptural stream dealing with the neutralisation of poison by Garuḍa mantras; its lore survives partly in later compilations and in regional poison-healing traditions.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08; low certainty on which surviving texts belong here. The Pāñcarātra Kāśyapa Saṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava analogue (listed for cross-reference only). family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism (Caitanya Sampradāya; Acintya Bhedābheda)

tradition.text: Caitanya appeared at Navadvīpa on Phālguna Pūrṇimā, Śaka 1407 (1486 CE), as Kṛṣṇa himself in the mood of Rādhā

scholarly.text: founded early 16th c. CE; theology systematised by the Vṛndāvana Gosvāmīs c. 1530–1600

transmissions_received.what: a guru-paramparā through Mādhavendra Purī and Īśvara Purī traced to Madhva
transmissions_received.evidence: Kavikarṇapūra's Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā; Baladeva's Prameyaratnāvalī (tradition's account; contested by scholars)

transmissions_received.what: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa as the 'spotless Purāṇa' and supreme pramāṇa
transmissions_received.evidence: Tattvasandarbha

transmissions_received.what: the rasa framework of Bharata's school, recast as bhakti-rasa
transmissions_received.evidence: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu; Ujjvalanīlamaṇi

transmissions_received.what: deity-worship and initiation ritual
transmissions_received.evidence: Haribhaktivilāsa

transmissions_given.what: Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa theology and the rasa vocabulary, reinterpreted (Sahajiyā use is rejected by the Gosvāmī orthodoxy)
Vaiṣṇava vocabulary of love and the name

distinctive_positions: Inconceivable difference-and-non-difference (acintya-bhedābheda) between the Lord and his powers (śakti), souls and world.
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself (svayaṃ bhagavān, BhP 1.3.28); the one non-dual reality is called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11), Bhagavān being fullest.
Three powers: internal (svarūpa/cit: sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), marginal (taṭasthā: the souls) and external (māyā).
Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa's hlādinī-śakti and the peak of love (mahābhāva); Caitanya is Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one form.
Pure devotion (uttamā bhakti) is the means and prema is the supreme goal (the 'fifth aim' beyond mokṣa).
Devotion is a rasa: five primary (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, mādhurya) and seven secondary rasas.
Practice (sādhana-bhakti) is rule-based (vaidhī) or spontaneous, following the Vraja residents (rāgānugā); stages from faith to love (BRS 1.4.15–16).

Congregational chanting of the name (nāma-saṅkīrtana), above all the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra, is the dharma of the Kali age; the name is non-different from Kṛṣṇa; ten offences against the name are to be avoided.
Rūpa and Viśvanātha hold paramour love (parakīyā) of the gopīs to be the highest; Jīva holds it to be svakīyā in truth — a recorded internal debate.
Caste and birth do not bar one from being a teacher of Kṛṣṇa (CC 2.8.128).
summary: The devotional tradition that grew from Caitanya (1486–1533) of Navadvīpa and Purī, his associates Nityānanda and Advaita, and the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana, who gave it a theology (Jīva's Ṣaṭ Sandarbha: acintya-bhedābheda), an aesthetics of devotion (Rūpa's Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi), a ritual code (Haribhaktivilāsa) and a hagiography (Caitanya Caritāmṛta, Caitanya Bhāgavata). Its practice centres on chanting the divine name, deity service, hearing the Bhāgavata, residence in Vraja and meditative participation in Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's eternal play.

name: Kālāmukha
regions: Karnataka (Balligāve/Belagāmi in Shimoga district and many other sites)

scholarly.text: c. 9th–14th c.; most inscriptions 11th–13th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Lākula doctrine and observance
transmissions_received.evidence: inscriptions describe Kālāmukha ācāryas as masters of the Lakula-siddhānta; scholarly identification

transmissions_given.what: temples and monasteries, possibly also members (disputed; see brw:kalamukha-to-virasaiva)

distinctive_positions: A temple- and monastery-based Śaiva order: its ācāryas served as temple heads and royal preceptors (rājaguru), and their maṭhas were centres of learning and charity (inscriptions).
Organised in 'assemblies' (pariṣad): the Śakti-pariṣad, whose chief seat was the Kōḍiya-maṭha of the Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāve, and the Siṃha-pariṣad.
Inscriptions praise its ācāryas as learned in the Lakula-siddhānta, Pātañjala yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Sāṃkhya, Buddhist doctrine, grammar and poetry.
Opponents (Yāmuna; Rāmānuja) report that they eat from a skull, bathe in and eat the ash of corpses, carry a club, and set up a pot of liquor and worship the deity placed in it.
summary: The Kālāmukhas are the Śaiva ascetics of numerous Karnataka inscriptions of the 11th–13th centuries, where they appear as learned heads of temples and monasteries, above all at Balligāve. Scholarship identifies them with the Lākula division of the Atimārga. Vaiṣṇava opponents describe skull and corpse-ash practices under their name. They disappear from the record by the 14th–15th century; how far their institutions passed to the Vīraśaivas is disputed.

name: Kālīkula (the Kālī lineages)
alt_names: Uttarāmnāya (the Northern transmission, in the āmnāya scheme)

tradition.text: Revealed by Śiva as Mahākāla/Bhairava to the Goddess; the tantras present themselves as eternal and as the scripture proper to the Kali age

scholarly.text: Kālī as a goddess in the Devī Māhātmya (c. 5th–6th c.); the Kashmirian Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala) c. 9th–10th c.; the eastern Kālī tantras mostly c. 14th–18th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Yāmala cults of fierce goddesses and the cremation-ground observances
transmissions_received.evidence: Jayadrathayāmala as a Vidyāpīṭha Yāmala (U08, U19)

transmissions_received.what: kaulācāra, the five tattvas, the bhāvas and the āmnāya scheme
transmissions_received.evidence: Kulārṇava and Kaulāvalīnirṇaya are cited throughout the eastern Kālī digests

transmissions_received.what: Kālī as the power of time and cognition (the twelve Kālīs)
transmissions_received.evidence: shared Kālīkula scripture (Jayadrathayāmala, Kālīkulapañcaśataka)

transmissions_given.what: the Dakṣiṇakālī cult, the Mahāvidyā system and Kālī-pūjā
Kālī worship at Dakshineswar as practised by Ramakrishna (recent)
Kālī as a village and temple goddess (documented only in part)

distinctive_positions: Kālī devours (kalana) time itself: Mahākāla is so called because he devours all beings, and she is the primordial Kālikā because she devours Mahākāla (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32).
Without Śakti Śiva is a corpse (śava): this is why Kālī stands upon Sadāśiva lying as a corpse (Toḍala 1.20-25).
In herself the Goddess is formless; her terrible cremation-ground form is imagined according to her qualities and acts for the benefit of worshippers (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-140; 13.5-13).
The ten Mahāvidyās are her forms, shown by Satī to Śiva (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa, Mahābhāgavata Purāṇa) and matched with Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (Toḍala 10.9-11).
Worship is graded by disposition (bhāva): paśu, vīra, divya; the Kālī tantras disagree whether vīra and divya worship is allowed in the Kali age (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3 against Mahānirvāṇa 5-8).
In Bengal the fierce Mother is approached with intimate devotion (Śyāmā-saṅgīt): the devotee may plead with, reproach and claim her as her child.
summary: The lineages that worship Kālī (and the goddesses of her 'family') as the supreme power. In Kashmir the Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala) fed the Krama; in Nepal the Uttarāmnāya worships Guhyakālī; in eastern India (Bengal, Assam, Mithilā) a large body of later tantras (Kālī, Toḍala, Nirvāṇa, Mahānirvāṇa, Kālīvilāsa, Niruttara, Kulacūḍāmaṇi, Śaktisaṅgama) and digests (Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra) teach the worship of Dakṣiṇakālī and the ten Mahāvidyās, by dakṣiṇa and vāma (Kaula) modes, which culminates in the Bengali Śākta devotional poetry of Rāmprasād and Kamalākānta.

name: Kāmaśāstra (the science of love and pleasure)
distinctive_positions: The three aims are to be pursued so that each supports and does not harm the others, distributed over a life of a hundred years; of dharma, artha and kāma each earlier one is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).
Kāma needs a śāstra because its right means must be learned; the text records and answers the Mīmāṃsaka and Lokāyatika objections (Kāmasūtra 1.2).
summary: The śāstra of the third aim of life (kāma), represented by Vātsyāyana Mallanāga's Kāmasūtra; recorded here only for its teaching on the three aims (trivarga) and its reported debate with Lokāyatikas.
notes: New lineage id (not in the registry) created by U02 for the puruṣārtha scope; the orchestrator may reassign.

name: Kāpālika (Somasiddhānta)

scholarly.text: possible earliest mention in Hāla's Sattasaī (anthology of uncertain date, early centuries CE onward); literary portraits c. 7th–11th c.; later references to c. 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the model of the skull-bearing penance for killing a brahmin
transmissions_received.evidence: Dharmaśāstra penance for brahmahatyā; Bhairava's penance in Kūrma P. 2.31 (scholarly hypothesis for the link)

transmissions_given.what: skull-bowl, skull-staff, bone ornaments and cremation-ground setting (disputed; see brw:kapalika-to-vajrayana)

distinctive_positions: The great vow (mahāvrata) of the skull, modelled on Bhairava's (Śiva's) penance for cutting off Brahmā's head (Kūrma P. 2.31): the ascetic lives as a Kapālin with a skull-bowl and skull-topped staff.

As reported by Yāmuna (Āgamaprāmāṇya) and Rāmānuja: liberation comes from knowing and wearing the six insignia (necklace/ear-ornament, rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash, sacred thread) with skull and khaṭvāṅga as sub-insignia, and from a meditation on the self seated in the yoni (opponents' report).
As reported: by mere entry into initiation one becomes a brahmin at once, and by taking the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic (Yāmuna, opponent's report).
Their doctrine is called Somasiddhānta; its content is not preserved.
Opponents' dramas portray Kāpālikas worshipping Bhairava and Cāmuṇḍā with liquor and alleged human offerings (Mālatīmādhava act 5; Prabodhacandrodaya act 3).
summary: The Kāpālikas, 'skull-men', were Śaiva ascetics who kept the great vow of the skull in imitation of Bhairava's penance. Their own scriptures are not identified; they are known through Purāṇic myth, Vaiṣṇava and Advaita polemic (Yāmuna, Rāmānuja, the Śaṅkaradigvijaya), Jain and Buddhist reports, and satirical or hostile portraits in Sanskrit drama (Mattavilāsa, Mālatīmādhava, Prabodhacandrodaya). Some sources group them with the Atimārga; others connect them with the Bhairava cults of the Mantramārga.
notes: Almost every statement about Kāpālika doctrine comes from opponents or satirists and is tagged reported_by_opponent. Continuity with later Aghorīs is a hypothesis, not a documented lineage.

name: Kashmir Śaivism (non-dual Śaiva tantra of Kashmir)
alt_names: Trika (in the broad sense used by Abhinavagupta and modern writers)
Īśvarādvayavāda (Utpaladeva's name for the non-duality of the Lord, Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti ch. 2)
regions: Jālandhara (seat of Abhinavagupta's Kaula teacher Śambhunātha)
South India / Cola country (Maheśvarānanda's Krama, c. 1300)

tradition.text: The Śaiva scriptures issue from Śiva's five faces; after they were lost at the start of the Kali age, Śiva as Śrīkaṇṭha commissioned Durvāsas to restore them (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-111); the Śiva Sūtras were revealed to Vasugupta on Mahādeva mountain.

scholarly.text: c. 850 CE (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa) - 11th c. classical period (Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, Kṣemarāja); commentarial and devotional continuation to the 18th-19th c.; revived in the 20th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Bhairava tantras (Svacchanda, Netra, Mālinīvijayottara, Siddhayogeśvarīmata) as scriptural base; the 36 tattvas, the three malas, śaktipāta and dīkṣā
transmissions_received.evidence: Kṣemarāja's Svacchandoddyota and Netroddyota; Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka built on the Mālinīvijayottara (TĀ 1.18)

transmissions_received.what: Kaula ritual and the kula/akula doctrine, via Śambhunātha of Jālandhara
transmissions_received.evidence: Tantrāloka 29; TĀ 5.52 (the seven ānandas as taught by Śambhu[nātha])

transmissions_received.what: Bhartṛhari's doctrine of speech (vāc) and pratibhā, reworked as vimarśa = supreme speech
transmissions_received.evidence: ĪPK 1.5.13; Śivadṛṣṭi ch. 2 critique

transmissions_received.what: the epistemological framework and vocabulary of Dharmakīrti's school, engaged polemically
transmissions_received.evidence: ĪPK 1.2 (Buddhist pūrvapakṣa), 1.6, 2.3

transmissions_given.what: prakāśa-vimarśa metaphysics and Spanda/Pratyabhijñā exegesis used by Śrīvidyā commentators (e.g. Jayaratha's Vāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa; Maheśvarānanda)
Abhinavagupta's aesthetics (rasa as relished consciousness; śānta rasa)
the oral and textual lineage continued in the 20th c. by Swami Lakshmanjoo

distinctive_positions: Reality is one consciousness (saṃvit, citi), Paramaśiva, whose nature is light (prakāśa) inseparably joined with reflexive awareness (vimarśa); an awareness without vimarśa would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).

The world is a real manifestation (ābhāsa) of that consciousness by its own freedom (svātantrya), displayed on its own screen (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 2) - not an illusory appearance (Advaita's vivarta) and not a separate matter.

Bondage is the contraction of consciousness through the three impurities; the root impurity is ignorance, not a substance (TĀ 1.22-23 citing the Mālinīvijayottara); liberation is recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Śiva.
Knowledge (jñāna) is the sole cause of liberation; ritual and yoga are means graded to the recipient's grace.
The thirty-six tattvas (Śiva to earth), extending Sāṃkhya's twenty-five with the pure principles and the five kañcukas.
Four means (upāya): anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava - graded by the intensity of the descent of grace (śaktipāta).
Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) with full activity in the world; the liberated sees the world as his own play.
Śiva performs five acts (emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace); the bound individual also performs them (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 10-11).
Spanda: the ultimate is dynamic vibration, the opening and closing of Śaṅkara's eyes (Spandakārikā 1.1).
Kaula ritual, including its antinomian elements, is interpreted by Abhinavagupta as an expression and means of non-dual consciousness (TĀ 29) - summary only.
summary: The non-dual Śaiva exegetical tradition of Kashmir (9th-11th c. classical period) that interpreted the Bhairava and Kaula tantras (Mālinīvijayottara, Svacchanda, Netra, Vijñāna Bhairava, Parātrīśikā) through four interlocking systems - Spanda (Vasugupta, Kallaṭa), Pratyabhijñā (Somānanda, Utpaladeva), Trika (culminating in Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka) and Krama (the Kālī-centred Mahānaya) - with the Kula and the little-known Mata alongside. It teaches that the self is Śiva, the world his free self-manifestation, bondage a contraction and liberation its recognition, attained by four graded means. Continued by Kṣemarāja, Jayaratha, the Kashmiri devotional poets (Lal Ded, Rūpa Bhavānī, Sāhib Kaul) and, recently, Swami Lakshmanjoo.
notes: 'Kashmir Śaivism' is a modern umbrella name; the tradition itself speaks of Trika, Ṣaḍardha, Pratyabhijñā, Spanda, Krama, Kula. Parent set to the Mantramārga because its scriptures are Bhairava tantras of the Mantramārga; its Kaula side derives from the Kulamārga (lin:kaula).

name: Kaula (the Kula tradition)

tradition.text: The Kaula teaching was brought down (avatārita) at Candradvīpa by Matsyendra (Macchaghna), and was taught earlier in each age by Siddhas (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.8-9; 22.10-12)

scholarly.text: Kaula scriptures from c. 9th–10th c. (Kaulajñānanirṇaya; the Kula stratum of the Trika); the Kulārṇava is usually placed c. 11th–14th c. (Muktabodha catalogue: 'post-1100')

transmissions_received.what: the yoginī cults and cremation-ground rites of the Yāmala tantras
transmissions_received.evidence: shared rites and the yoginī-kaula (U08, U19)

transmissions_received.what: Kāpālika observances, reinterpreted as inner and domestic worship
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly hypothesis

transmissions_given.what: Kula ritual and doctrine integrated by Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 29)
kaulācāra and the five tattvas in Kālī worship
the Kaula mode of Śrīvidyā worship
Matsyendra's Kaula teaching as the root of the Nāth lineage (tradition's account)

distinctive_positions: Kula is Śakti and Akula is Śiva; the Kaulas are skilled in joining kula and akula (Kulārṇava 17.27).
Kaula is the highest of the seven modes of conduct: Veda < Vaiṣṇava < Śaiva < Dakṣiṇa < Vāma < Siddhānta < Kaula (Kulārṇava 2.7-8).
In the Kula dharma enjoyment itself becomes yoga, sin becomes merit and saṃsāra becomes liberation (Kulārṇava 2.23-24).
The Kula truth is beyond both duality and non-duality (Kulārṇava 1.110).
The body is the temple and the jīva is Sadāśiva; bound it is jīva, freed it is Śiva (Kulārṇava 9.41-43).
The teaching passes only from ear to ear from a tested guru to a tested disciple, never to the deceitful (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 6.9-14; Kulārṇava 14.19, 14.25).

Worship with the kula substances (summary only) is held to reveal the bliss of Brahman latent in the body, and is condemned when done for pleasure or without initiation (Kulārṇava 2.117; 5.79-80; 5.99; 5.104).
In the circle of worship (bhairavīcakra) all castes are twice-born; outside it they are separate (Kulārṇava 8.96-97).
summary: The Kaula or Kula tradition teaches the worship of the Goddess and her 'family' (kula) of powers — the yoginīs and mothers — together with Bhairava, as a path of both enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). Its early scripture is the Kaulajñānanirṇaya ascribed to Matsyendra; its classic later exposition is the Kulārṇava Tantra (17 ullāsas) on the guru, initiation, the āmnāyas, the seven ullāsas and the Kula worship with the five tattvas; it branches into the four or five āmnāyas (Kubjikā's Paścimāmnāya, the Kālī Uttarāmnāya, Śrīvidyā's Dakṣiṇāmnāya, the Pūrva and Ūrdhva), shaped the Trika of Abhinavagupta and the eastern Kālī and Tārā cults, and insists on secrecy, the guru's authority and graded eligibility.

name: Kaula Śrīvidyā (the Vāmakeśvara–Yoginīhṛdaya exegetical line)

tradition.text: The teaching descends from Śiva (Parameśvara) through the divine, perfected and human streams of gurus.

scholarly.text: Puṇyānanda and Amṛtānanda c. 13th-14th c. (uncertain); Bhāskararāya and Umānandanātha 18th c.

transmissions_received.what: Kaula conduct and ritual frame
transmissions_received.evidence: Yoginīhṛdaya Dīpikā on 2.81 (kaulācāra); Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra 1.12, 1.24

distinctive_positions: Outer worship of the cakra is performed even by the omniscient Śiva because it leads to the knowledge of non-difference (Yoginīhṛdaya 3.3 with the Dīpikā); inner and outer worship together.

Bliss is the form of Brahman, present in the body; the five 'M's manifest it and are used in secret; exposure leads to hell; when they are unavailable the daily worship continues without them (PKS 1.12, 1.24).
The Goddess is at once Kaula and Samaya (Bhāskararāya on Lalitā Sahasranāma 36-37).
Initiation in stages (Bālā first, then the higher vidyās) with initiatory names ending in '-ānandanātha' (PKS 1.39-41).
The Vedic standing of Śrīvidyā is defended by Mīmāṃsā reasoning (Bhāskararāya).
summary: The line of Śrīvidyā that follows the Vāmakeśvara tantra and Yoginīhṛdaya within a Kaula frame: Puṇyānanda's Kāmakalāvilāsa, Amṛtānanda's Dīpikā, the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra with Umānandanātha's Nityotsava, and Bhāskararāya's commentaries. It combines outer Śrīcakra worship, Kaula conduct kept secret, and non-dual knowledge.
notes: 'Kaula Śrīvidyā' is a descriptive grouping used here for the Kaula-affiliated exegetical line; the texts call their conduct kaulācāra. Many living lines practise its rites with substitutes (dakṣiṇa mode).

name: Kerala tantra (temple-tantra tradition of Kerala)

scholarly.text: the Tantrasamuccaya is a 15th-c. work; the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is older (c. 11th–12th c.); the Prapañcasāra and Śāradātilaka are earlier pan-Indian mantra manuals used in Kerala

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva Siddhānta ritual via the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: Viṣṇu ritual
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis

transmissions_received.what: mantra procedures of the Prapañcasāra and the Śāradātilaka
transmissions_received.evidence: tradition-account

distinctive_positions: Temple worship is conducted according to tantra texts, above all the Tantrasamuccaya, by hereditary Nampūtiri brahmin tantri families who alone perform installations (pratiṣṭhā), festivals (utsava) and the major purifications.
The Tantrasamuccaya treats the installation and worship of seven deities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa, Durgā, Subrahmaṇya, Gaṇapati and Śāstā.
Daily worship is performed by resident priests (śānti) under the tantri's authority; the day is structured by a series of pūjās and processional offerings (śīveli).
Kerala tantra combines Vedic (smārta) Nampūtiri practice with Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta tantric procedures.
summary: Kerala's temple-tantra tradition is the body of ritual texts and hereditary tantri lineages that govern temple building, installation, daily worship, festivals and purification in Kerala's Hindu temples. Its central text is Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan's Tantrasamuccaya, supported by the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, the Prapañcasāra, the Śāradātilaka and Malayalam manuals.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority. Tantri families named in REPORT.md (Cēnnās, Taraṇanallūr, Tāḻaman) are given with moderate/low confidence and not as separate lineages.

name: Krama (the 'Sequence'; Mahānaya, Mahārtha)
regions: Oḍḍiyāna (in the tradition's account of Jñānanetra's revelation)

tradition.text: Revealed by the goddess to Jñānanetra (Śivānanda) - the tradition's account.

scholarly.text: Kālīkula scriptures (Jayadrathayāmala etc.) before c. 900; Kashmirian Krama c. 850-1000; Maheśvarānanda c. 1300; Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa later.

transmissions_received.what: the Kālīkula scriptures and the cult of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī
transmissions_received.evidence: Jayadrathayāmala; Kālīkulapañcaśataka

transmissions_given.what: the twelve Kālīs integrated as a form of śāktopāya (TĀ 4.148-172)
Krama ideas in Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī, which also draws on Śrīvidyā

distinctive_positions: Worship and contemplation of Kālī as the power that 'counts', emits and devours (kalana) all things; the five senses of the root kal: projecting, knowing, counting, moving, sounding (TĀ 4.173).

The twelve Kālīs as the phases of every act of cognition - emission, persistence, withdrawal and the nameless (anākhya) - across object, means of knowledge and knowing subject (TĀ 4.148-172; Abhinavagupta's Kramastotra).
The five flows (pañcavāha) of goddesses: Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī, Bhūcarī (low confidence).
Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, 'she who draws in time', is supreme.
The sequence (krama) of cognition leads into the sequenceless (akrama).
summary: The Kālī-centred Kaula tradition of the northern transmission as practised in Kashmir (Mahānaya, Mahārtha), rooted in the Jayadrathayāmala and related Kālīkula scriptures and said to have been revealed to Jñānanetra. Abhinavagupta absorbed its doctrine of the twelve Kālīs into the Trika (TĀ 4; Kramastotra); Maheśvarānanda's Mahārthamañjarī and Śitikaṇṭha's Mahānayaprakāśa are later statements. Much of its scripture survives only in manuscript or citation.
notes: Parent set to the Kashmirian grouping; historically a Kālīkula (lin:kalikula) Kaula system.

name: Kubjikā tradition (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission')
regions: the western Himalaya (Oḍḍiyāna, in the tradition's account)
Konkan and the Deccan (Candradvīpa / Śrīśaila in the tradition's geography)

tradition.text: The Goddess received the transmission at Candradvīpa and spread it from the western Himalaya (the 'western' of all paths) to Śrīśaila, Kiṣkindhā and Oḍḍiyāna (Kubjikāmata 2.20-40)

scholarly.text: Kubjikāmata perhaps c. 10th c. or earlier; the Kubjikā cult survives in Nepal among Newar tantric priests

transmissions_received.what: the Kaula yoginī and siddha framework
transmissions_received.evidence: the Kubjikāmata calls itself the Kulālikāmnāya

transmissions_received.what: the Mālinī letter-order and Trika goddess mantras
transmissions_received.evidence: KMT ch. 4-5 (Mālinī), Goudriaan–Schoterman edition

transmissions_given.what: shared ritual culture of Newar tantric priests (Kubjikā worship in Bhaktapur and Kathmandu)
cakra vocabulary and Siddha lists shared with the Nāth tradition (scholarly hypothesis)

distinctive_positions: The Goddess Kubjikā ('the Bent One') emerged from the liṅga, dark and hunch-backed, and became bent out of shame (lajjā) when Bhairava asked for the transmission (Kubjikāmata 2.3-5, 2.14).
Śiva and the Goddess are mutually dependent: 'nothing is without me, nothing without you'; Bhairava calls her his guru (Kubjikāmata 2.17-18).
The four seats are four levels of the supreme yoni: Kāmākhya (beyond form), Pūrṇagiri (form), Jālandhara (word), Oḍra/Oḍḍiyāna (body) (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).
The six centres (ṣaṭprakāra, with their goddesses) are the body of the Goddess; Kubjikā is the coiled power (Kubjikāmata 2.2 hymn; chs. 11-15).
The disciple who breaks the samayas and slanders the guru becomes 'dead while living' (Kubjikāmata 12.3-9).
summary: Kubjikā ('the Bent One', Kujā), consort of Navātman/Kujeśa Bhairava, is the goddess of the Paścimāmnāya, the western of the Kaula transmissions. Its root scripture, the Kubjikāmata (25 paṭalas, c. 3,500 verses in the Kulālikāmnāya recension), with the Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā and the vast Manthānabhairava, teaches the Goddess's descent through the sacred seats, a mantra-maṇḍala system of six centres and their yoginīs, and strict samaya discipline. Absorbed into the Kālī and Śrīvidyā cults elsewhere, it survives as a living cult in Nepal.

name: Lākula
regions: known through Kashmirian and Nepalese scriptural sources

scholarly.text: attested in Śaiva scriptures from c. 6th–7th c. (Niśvāsa corpus) and, as Kālāmukhas, in inscriptions c. 9th–14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Pāśupata base of observance and doctrine
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly reconstruction from the Niśvāsamukha and later Śaiva sources

transmissions_given.what: the Lākula doctrine (inscriptions praise Kālāmukha ācāryas as learned in the 'Lakula-siddhānta')

distinctive_positions: Its observance is the great vow (mahāvrata), also called the skull observance (kapālavrata) or observance 'beyond the world' (lokātīta): the ascetic carries a human skull as his bowl and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and smears himself with ash (as described in Śaiva scriptures; details reconstructed).
The Svacchanda Tantra names the skull-observers (kapālavratin) beside the Pāśupatas as those who stand 'in the Īśvara and in the Dhruva' and are not re-created (11.184).
It is described by scholarship as a system intermediate between Pāñcārthika Pāśupatism and the Mantramārga, with its own hierarchy of worlds; its scriptures are lost.
summary: The Lākulas form the second division of the Atimārga. They are known almost only through the Mantramārga scriptures that describe them (the Niśvāsamukha, the Svacchanda Tantra) and through the Kālāmukhas of Karnataka inscriptions, whom scholarship identifies with them. Their observance was the great vow of the skull, 'beyond the world'. No Lākula scripture survives complete.
notes: Low confidence throughout; reconstruction depends on A. Sanderson's work on the Niśvāsamukha and the Lākulas (scholarly metadata only).

name: Mantramārga (the Path of Mantras)
alt_names: mantra-tantra (Kāmika's name for the fifth stream)
regions: Cambodia (Khmer inscriptions record Śaiva tantric texts)

tradition.text: revealed by Śiva/Sadāśiva through his five faces at the beginning of creation and handed down through chains of divine and semi-divine transmitters (tantrāvatāra; Kāmika pūrva 1; Kiraṇa vidyāpāda 10)

scholarly.text: earliest surviving scripture (core of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā) c. 450–550 CE; most major scriptures c. 6th–10th c.; systematic exegesis 7th–12th c.

transmissions_received.what: Śaiva ascetic observances, the five brahma-mantras and the Pāśupata heritage
transmissions_received.evidence: scholarly-hypothesis (the Niśvāsa and later texts present the Atimārga as the prior, lower Śaiva path; historians such as A. Sanderson treat the Mantramārga as having developed after it)

transmissions_given.what: the yoginī cults of the Vidyāpīṭha, reformulated in the Kaula traditions
Śaiva ritual procedures via paddhatis such as the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati
Vīraśaiva recensions of Siddhānta scriptures (e.g. Candrajñāna, Makuṭa, Vīra)

distinctive_positions: Scripture is revealed by Sadāśiva through five faces as five streams: Siddhānta (upper face), Gāruḍa (east), Vāma (north), Bhūta (west) and Bhairava (south) (Kāmika pūrva 1.20–27).

Knowledge is twofold by eligibility: Śiva's knowledge (śivajñāna), revealing the Lord, is the higher; the Veda and the rest, revealing the bound soul and its bonds, are the lower (Kāmika pūrva 1.14–17).
Religion is graded as worldly (laukika), Vedic (vaidika), spiritual (ādhyātmika: Sāṃkhya-Yoga), the Atimārga and the Mantramārga, the last being highest (Niśvāsamukha; Kāmika pūrva 1.17–19).
Initiation (dīkṣā) is a rite on the soul, not on caste or body; liberation comes through it (Kiraṇa 6.3–9).
The Mantramārga offers both supernatural powers/enjoyments (bhukti) and liberation (mukti), to householders as well as ascetics; initiates are graded samayin, putraka, sādhaka and ācārya.

The Siddhānta's 28 scriptures (10 Śivabheda, 18 Rudrabheda) and the 64 Bhairava tantras (eight groups of eight) are all Śiva's teaching; the Kashmirian exegetes rank them as teaching difference, difference-in-identity and non-difference respectively (Tantrāloka 1.18 with Jayaratha).
Worship is performed with mantras through which the deity is present; the officiant first purifies himself, the place, the substances, the mantras and the liṅga (Kāmika pūrva 4.37–38).
summary: The Mantramārga is the initiatory, mantra-based division of Śaivism, distinguished in its own scriptures (Niśvāsa, Kāmika) from the ascetic Atimārga. It comprises the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta with its 28 scriptures and their upāgamas, and the non-Saiddhāntika tantras: the Bhairava tantras (Mantrapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha), the Vāma tantras of Tumburu, and the Gāruḍa and Bhūta tantras. It teaches initiation, daily and temple worship, mantra-practice for powers, and yoga, as means to both enjoyment and liberation.
notes: family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority. Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine is owned by U18, Kashmir traditions by U19, Śākta by U23/U24; this entry covers the division and its scriptural catalogue.

name: Mantrapīṭha (the Seat of Mantras)

scholarly.text: the Svacchandatantra predates the 10th c. (commented on by Kṣemarāja, 11th c.; known to Abhinavagupta)

distinctive_positions: The Bhairava tantras of the southern stream divide into the Mantrapīṭha and the Vidyāpīṭha; in the Mantrapīṭha the central deity is a male Bhairava, above all Svacchandabhairava with his consort Aghoreśvarī.
The first group of the 64 Bhairava tantras in the Śrīkaṇṭhīya list (the Bhairavāṣṭaka) opens with the Svacchanda and was 'spoken by Bahurūpa' (Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18).
summary: Division of the Bhairava tantras centred on a male Bhairava (chiefly Svacchandabhairava). Its main surviving scripture, the Svacchandatantra with Kṣemarāja's Uddyota, shaped Kashmirian Śaiva ritual.
notes: Sub-lineage created by U08 for the Mantramārga's internal division (not in the registry). The Netratantra (Amṛteśvara/Mṛtyuñjaya cult) is listed here provisionally; its classification is not settled here. family 'vedic' is the project's A/B classification (Brahmanical vs śramaṇa); it is not a claim that this tradition treats the Veda as its final authority.

name: Mata (the 'Doctrine'; the Mata scriptures)
regions: Kashmir (as known to Abhinavagupta and Jayaratha)

scholarly.text: Known only through references by Abhinavagupta (c. 1000) and Jayaratha (13th c.); origin and dates unknown.

distinctive_positions: Its scriptures (mataśāstra) reject the samaya observances and similar rules as based on difference, teaching instead that one's own awareness, unbounded and complete, is to be realized (TĀ 4.262-263 with Jayaratha, who quotes the Mata line 'nirmaryādaṃ svasambodhaṃ sampūrṇaṃ budhyatām').
They forbid restricting eating and the worship of the cakra to members of one's own lineage (santāna), because such division fragments the undivided reality (TĀ 4.268-270).

In the Kashmirian scriptural hierarchy the Mata stands between the Dakṣiṇa (right-hand Bhairava) scriptures and the Kula (TĀ 13.300-301 and the verse quoted there by Jayaratha); a variant verse quoted in the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa places it after the Kula and just below the Trika.
summary: A Śaiva/Kaula scriptural tradition, now lost, that the Kashmirian exegetes count as one of the systems alongside Kula, Krama and Trika. What is known comes almost entirely from the Tantrāloka and Jayaratha's Viveka: its rejection of the samaya rules and of lineage-based exclusions, and its rank in the scriptural hierarchy. Its own texts, deities and teachers are not securely identified in this skeleton.
notes: Low confidence throughout. Jayaratha on TĀ 4.262 calls the Mata scriptures 'samaviṣamalakṣaṇa' - sense unclear. Modern scholarship (Sanderson) associates the Mata with a Kālīkula/northern-transmission cult; that identification is not asserted here and is listed as a gap.

name: Mīmāṃsā (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā)
regions: across the subcontinent; later centres of study at Vārāṇasī, Mithilā, and in South India (Tamil country, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra)

tradition.text: Jaimini, pupil of Vyāsa (Bādarāyaṇa), taught at the close of the Dvāpara age (the tradition's account)

scholarly.text: Mīmāṃsā Sūtra c. 3rd c. BCE – 1st c. CE (estimates vary widely); Śabara c. 3rd–5th c. CE; unbroken commentarial tradition to the present

transmissions_received.what: the śrauta ritual corpus and the Brāhmaṇa exegesis of injunction (vidhi) and explanatory praise (arthavāda) that Mīmāṃsā systematizes
transmissions_received.evidence: every adhikaraṇa of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra takes its topic (viṣaya) from Vedic ritual texts

transmissions_received.what: procedural knowledge of the kalpa (śrauta) sūtras and grammatical analysis of Vedic words
transmissions_received.evidence: Śabara and Kumārila cite kalpa-sūtras and discuss the authority of grammar (MS 1.3.24–29; Tantravārttika vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa)

transmissions_given.what: the adhikaraṇa method, rules of textual interpretation (the basis of the six marks of purport), and — for Advaita — the Bhāṭṭa account of the means of knowledge in empirical matters
interpretive maxims (nyāya) used by Dharmaśāstra commentators and digest writers
the teaching (via the Vṛttikāra cited by Rāmānuja) that Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā form one continuous śāstra; Vedānta Deśika's theistic reading of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra

distinctive_positions: Dharma is a beneficial object known only through Vedic injunction (codanā); perception and reasoning based on it cannot know dharma (MS 1.1.2, 1.1.4).
The relation of word and meaning is original (autpattika), not made by any person; hence the Veda's injunctions are a self-sufficient means of knowledge (MS 1.1.5).
Words (letters) are eternal; utterance only manifests them (MS 1.1.6–23).
The Veda is authorless (apauruṣeya) and beginningless; names attached to its recensions derive from their expounders (MS 1.1.27–32).
Every cognition is valid of itself; invalidity is established only by a defect in its cause or a later contradicting cognition (svataḥ-prāmāṇya).
The Veda consists of injunction, mantra, name, prohibition and explanatory praise; all of it is meaningful through connection with injunctions (MS 1.2.7).
A ritual act, though perishable, produces an unseen potency (apūrva) that yields the promised result later (MS 2.1.5 with Śabara).
The sacrificial act, not the deity, is principal; the deity is that to which the offering is directed as named in the injunction or mantra (MS 9.1.9).
No creator god and no total creation or dissolution of the world are established by any means of knowledge (Kumārila; Śālikanātha).
No person — human, yogin or god — perceives dharma directly; claims of omniscience in matters of dharma are rejected (Kumārila).
Heaven (svarga) is the original declared goal of Vedic rites; later teachers add liberation (mokṣa) as the ending of embodiment through the exhaustion of karma.
